---
title: Model comparisons
---

The first experiment compares team-only, player-only, and combined lineup forecasts
on future ODI matches. Read the [experiment specification](lineup_experiment.qmd)
for cutoffs, shrinkage, uncertainty, independent review, and interpretation limits.
Rendering reads the saved publication and does not refit models.

{{< include ../out/release/lineup/report.md >}}

## Research sequence

| Stage | Purpose | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| International match and participant preparation | Stable identities, dated outcomes, and substitution flags | Implemented |
| Regularized lineup win/loss model | Outcome-based player benchmark | Implemented; saved pilot above |
| Player-only rankings by format | Five-year outcome associations for Tests, ODIs, and T20Is | [Published tables](ratings.qmd); exploratory |
| Ball-level runs and wickets | Contextual contribution estimates | Specification and estimation pending |
| Time-varying player strength | Current ability and future-match forecasts | Follows the initial benchmarks |
| Win probability added | Retrospective match impact | Follows a validated probability model |
| Replacement simulation | Counterfactual lineup selection | Deferred |

## Outcome-based benchmark

The player-model predictor is the sum of team A's player effects minus the sum of team
B's effects, plus context terms that reverse direction when the teams are swapped.
Shrinkage is needed because teammates often appear together. A coefficient is a
relative log-odds contribution, not a number of wins or a causal effect.

The first binary experiment uses decisive matches with unambiguous fixed
XIs. Preparation retains other outcomes and substitution matches with explicit
flags; later specifications may use them. Run margins and wicket margins are
different quantities and must not be combined as a response. A successful chase
also ends when the target is reached, truncating the observed scoring margin.

National-team strength and player strength are entangled. Team effects, time
windows, and priors affect how shared performance is allocated. Before interpreting
individual rankings, examine lineup overlap, weakly identified players, and
sensitivity to those choices. More deliveries do not create more independent
match outcomes for a lineup regression.

## Ball-level valuation

The model must account for the future cost of losing a wicket, as well as immediate
runs. One candidate values an event as runs scored plus the change in expected
remaining innings runs. Chases require target-aware valuation. Dismissal types,
extras, fielding credit, shortened matches, and exposure need explicit rules before
estimation. These are research specifications, not assumptions hidden in a parser.

## Evaluation and publication gates

- Use chronological future-match holdouts, tuning hyperparameters within earlier
  training periods. Keep all deliveries from a match in the same partition.
- Compare lineup forecasts against a team-only model on the same matches. Use
  dated `side_order` exports with documented match-ID mappings where applicable.
- Report log loss, Brier score, calibration, and uncertainty in score differences;
  account for dependence within series.
- Test sensitivity to regularization, time windows, team effects, replacement
  definitions, and sample restrictions. Show rank uncertainty and exposure.
- Assess men's and women's ODIs separately. Prediction quality alone does not
  establish that individual credit has been allocated correctly.
- Check models on simulated data with known player effects, including players
  who always appear together. The model must expose weak identification.

Time-varying strength becomes a published rating only after comparison with the
static and team-only benchmarks. A contribution measure becomes WAR only after
replacement and wins calibration are defended. Replacement probability differences
need not sum to the team's wins in a nonlinear model.
